clue.text: See 28
Single-stemmed plant's quality improved

parts.note: a level of quality, the benchmark in 'high ___s'
went up, got better, as prices or spirits do

explanation.surface: A gardener admiring how a single-stemmed plant has come on this season.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's name is split into two ordinary words, a noun and a past-tense verb, so the solver must read 'quality improved' as two separate pieces rather than a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard rose is a rose bush grafted and trained onto one tall bare stem, like a small tree.

clue.text: Question one: What might be said to end a ride?

definitions.text: What might be said to end a ride?

parts.note: a question word, as in 'who goes there?'
a = one, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A quiz host posing the first question, about how a journey comes to a stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Question one' looks like a quiz heading; it is really two pieces, WHO and A, and the rest is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Riders call this out to a horse to make it halt, so it is literally spoken to finish riding.

clue.text: Habitually fit some plastic to retain temperature

indicators.note: to retain is to keep inside, so the reshaped letters hold the temperature symbol
something plastic can be moulded into any shape, so the letters of 'fit some' get remoulded

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
T is the standard symbol for temperature

explanation.surface: Someone who routinely fits plastic insulation to keep the heat in.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of FIT SOME gives OFTIMES, itself a word for 'often', and T slips in after OF to make the longer archaic form.
explanation.definitionFit: Ofttimes is an old literary word meaning often or frequently, which is what habitual actions are.

clue.text: Nice way to support nut production? Wrong

indicators.note: a production of something remakes it, so the word 'nut' is reworked into a new order
in a down clue a supporting piece sits underneath, so the French street goes below the reworked nut

parts.note: the three letters of 'nut' rearranged
in Nice, the French city, a street is a rue

explanation.surface: A question about whether a road on the Riviera helps a nut-growing business, promptly dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' at the start of a sentence hides its capital: it is the French city, so its 'way' is French. In a down clue the supporting piece comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untrue is false or incorrect, a plain synonym for being in error.

clue.text: Christian making Satan a bit peeved at first

indicators.note: the loose letters are used as raw material for making something new, so they are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

indicators.note: 'at first' asks for only the opening letter of the word before it, 'peeved'

parts.note: the first letter of 'peeved'

explanation.surface: A believer who has managed to get the Devil mildly annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: Satan is the last thing to expect in the fodder for a Christian; the letter from 'peeved' completes the ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Anabaptists are a Protestant movement practising adult baptism, from whom Mennonites and Amish descend.

clue.text: Imitate Spanish artist capturing Republican revolutionary leader

indicators.note: to capture is to take in, so the painter's name holds the Republican

parts.note: Joan Miró, the Spanish surrealist painter
R is the usual abbreviation for Republican

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of 'revolutionary' is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of 'revolutionary'

explanation.surface: A Spanish painter copying the style of a Republican revolutionary figure, as in a political portrait.
explanation.walkthrough: The Republican goes inside the artist's name, between I and R, and the revolutionary's initial is tacked on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To mirror someone is to copy their actions exactly, as a reflection does.

clue.text: Fine plant for skin

parts.note: F = fine, as on pencil grades
to plant something is to set it down, to lay it

explanation.surface: A gardening or cosmetics tip about a good herb for the complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' and 'skin' both read as nouns in the surface; both are verbs in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To flay an animal is to strip off its hide, so it is the verb meaning remove the outer covering.

clue.text: A yearning for hope initially

parts.note: used as printed
an itch is a restless longing, as in an itch to travel

explanation.surface: Someone who, at the start, hopes and longs for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope initially' looks like an instruction to take a first letter; here it is the definition, naming that letter as a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aitch is the spelled-out name of the letter H, which begins the word hope.

clue.text: About ready to flip, if ditched in canal

indicators.note: flipping something turns it round, so the little word 'if' is read backwards

parts.note: used as printed, then turned round

indicators.note: a ditched car is wrecked, so the letters of 'in canal' end up out of order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A boat or car nearly ready to tip over, if it ends up dumped in the canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About ready' reads as 'almost prepared'; ready is British slang for cash (short for ready money), so it means concerning money.
explanation.definitionFit: Financial means relating to money, and 'ready' is informal British slang for cash, so 'about ready' is money matters.

clue.text: One who survives embracing political party that bombed

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so the survivor wraps round the party

parts.note: one who lasts, a survivor
the African National Congress, South Africa's governing party

explanation.surface: A survivor who belonged to a political party that crashed at the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombed' suggests an electoral flop; it is literal, pointing to the Second World War aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avro Lancaster was the RAF's main heavy bomber of the Second World War, so it is a thing that dropped bombs.

clue.text: Crazy but well

parts.note: but = bar, both meaning except, as in 'all bar one'
well and my are both mild exclamations of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like someone's mental state described as mad yet healthy; both small words are really synonyms. Barmy is everyday British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is informal British slang for foolish or mad, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Brit absorbing 'hard worker' spirit

indicators.note: absorbing means soaking up inside, so the Brit takes the worker into the middle

parts.note: Pom is Australian slang for a British person
H = hard, as on pencils
the crossword's standard worker insect

explanation.surface: A British spirits drinker downing something labelled for hard workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' at the end suggests alcohol after 'absorbing'; it is a ghost.
explanation.definitionFit: A phantom is a ghost or apparition, which is one sense of a spirit.

clue.text: Old writer holding lives in balance

indicators.note: holding something means keeping it inside, so the old writer's name keeps the verb within it

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the 19th-century American writer
lives = is, exists

explanation.surface: A writer of the past with people's lives hanging in the balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lives' looks like the plural noun; it is the verb, so it means exists.
explanation.definitionFit: Poise is steadiness and equilibrium, a synonym of balance as a noun.

clue.text: Car, jet brazenly parked on politician's path!

indicators.note: in a down clue what is parked on top sits above, so the jumbled vehicles come before the politician
acting brazenly means behaving wildly and without restraint, so those letters are thrown about

parts.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters
a Tory is a member of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: An outraged report of vehicles left blocking an MP's footpath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Path' reads as the pavement being obstructed; it is the curve something follows through the air.
explanation.definitionFit: A trajectory is the course a moving object, such as a missile, follows through space.

clue.text: Lover, once having pried, turned and ran out

parts.note: a former partner is an ex

indicators.note: turned here means changed round, so the letters of 'pried' are mixed

parts.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

explanation.surface: A former partner who snooped, then spun round and fled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran out' reads as fleeing the room; it means came to an end, as a passport or contract does.
explanation.definitionFit: Expired means came to the end of its validity, the same as a licence that has run out.

clue.text: On a regular basis, a diver may be heard

indicators.note: only what is heard counts, so the diver's surname stands in by its sound alone

parts.note: Tom Daley, the British Olympic champion diver

explanation.surface: A diver whose splashes can be heard regularly at the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Daley is Britain's best-known diver, an Olympic gold medallist famous since his teens.
explanation.definitionFit: Daily means every day, which is a regular routine repeated at set intervals.

clue.text: Nation elected to get back funds

parts.note: a winning candidate is in

indicators.note: getting back means going in the opposite direction, so the word for funds reads backwards

parts.note: aid is money given to help, as in foreign aid

explanation.surface: A country that voted in a new government to recover its money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get back' looks like recovering money; it turns the funds round.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a country in South Asia, so it is simply one example of a nation.

clue.text: Shiner causes squint oddly

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, first, third and fifth, of the word before it

parts.note: letters 1, 3 and 5 of 'squint'

explanation.surface: A black eye makes its owner squint in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: A shiner is slang for a black eye, and the surface depends on that; here it means something that shines.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun is the thing in the sky that shines, so it is literally a shiner, one who shines.

clue.text: Particle, negative, orbiting form of inert uranium

indicators.note: orbiting means circling round, so the negative word goes around the rest

parts.note: no is the negative answer

indicators.note: a new form of something is a reshaping, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder: 'inert' plus U, the symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Physics jargon: a negatively charged particle circling uranium.
explanation.walkthrough: The physics surface makes 'negative' look like electric charge; it simply means a refusal word.
explanation.definitionFit: A neutrino is a tiny subatomic particle with no charge and almost no mass.

clue.text: Sexual declaration used in poems?

definitions.note: read as the phrase 'I am bi'
definitions.meaning: split as three words, a statement of bisexuality

definitions.note: describes metrical feet, which are nouns
definitions.meaning: the plural of a metrical foot, a short syllable followed by a long

explanation.surface: Whether coming out as bisexual is something that appears in poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as three words the answer is 'I am bi'; read as one it is a Latin plural of iambus, the metrical foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Iambi are metrical feet of one unstressed then one stressed syllable, the basic unit of much English verse.

clue.text: Nautical remit: 'Aim to swim!'

indicators.note: swimming letters move about freely, so those of 'remit: aim' drift into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A naval instruction whose mission statement is simply to swim.
explanation.walkthrough: The seafaring surface is continuous with the definition, which makes it easy to overlook that 'swim' is doing the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Maritime and nautical are synonyms, both describing ships, sailing and the sea.

clue.text: State calls for end of free vote petition

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only the final letter of 'free' is taken

parts.note: the last letter of 'free'
a cross on a ballot paper is a vote
to press is to urge or petition someone

explanation.surface: A government campaign demanding an end to free votes in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a nation; it is the verb to say.
explanation.definitionFit: To express something is to put it into words, which is to state it.

clue.text: Concert part for theatre assistant

parts.note: a Prom is one of the BBC's summer Promenade concerts in London
pt is the abbreviation for part

explanation.surface: A section of a concert programme reserved for a stagehand.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are a famous annual season of classical concerts at London's Royal Albert Hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A prompt is the person offstage who feeds actors their forgotten lines during a performance.

clue.text: Said dessert's a week's portion

indicators.note: 'said' means spoken, so the dessert counts only by how its name is pronounced

parts.note: an ice-cream sundae, with the 's joining it to the definition

explanation.surface: A claim that one pudding is someone's ration for the whole week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Portion' suggests a serving of the dessert; it means one of the seven parts of the week.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday is one of the seven days, so it is a single division of the week.

clue.text: Say one's left deposit, in full

parts.note: to say is to utter

indicators.note: 'one's left' means one has departed, so that article goes from the word for deposit

parts.note: to lay is to deposit, as a hen lays eggs
a = one, the indefinite article, which is removed

explanation.surface: A banking query about whether a deposit was left in full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example'; it is the verb. 'Left deposit' reads as money left behind, but 'one's left' is a departure.
explanation.definitionFit: Utterly means completely or totally, the adverb matching the phrase 'to the full extent'.

clue.text: Maybe squash plant variant?

definitions.meaning: squash, the racket game, is one example
botanists' term for a mutant shoot unlike its parent

explanation.walkthrough: Squash is also a vegetable, so 'squash plant' reads as one gardening phrase; the break falls between them.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany a sport is a spontaneous mutation, a branch differing from the rest of the plant; squash is a game played competitively.

clue.text: Row of bugs turned over

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, and in a down clue that reads the listening devices from bottom to top

parts.note: bugs and taps are both hidden listening devices on phones

explanation.surface: A line of insects lying on their backs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' and 'bugs' both look like a line of insects; they are a quarrel and wiretaps.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a petty quarrel, which is one meaning of a row (rhyming with cow).

clue.text: Hot tar's forced into near empty navigational aid

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it, so the jumble sits within the emptied word
an empty word has lost its contents, so only the outer letters of 'near' remain

parts.note: 'near' with its middle removed

indicators.note: something forced has been pushed out of shape, so the letters of 'hot tar's' are jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Road workers pouring hot tar into a nearly empty space around a sign.
explanation.walkthrough: The roadworks picture makes 'navigational aid' sound like a road sign; it is a star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris, the star nearly above the celestial pole, has guided sailors north for centuries.

clue.text: Malicious stuff, the crap about a 'jumped-up' Brit band member

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled word goes around the single letter
crap here is an adjective for poor or messed up, so the letters of 'the' are scrambled

parts.note: anagram fodder, 3 letters
used as printed

indicators.note: jumped up means going upward, and in a down clue that reads the band member backwards

parts.note: Liam Gallagher, singer of the British rock band Oasis

explanation.surface: A rant about the rubbish spread by an arrogant member of a Britpop band.
explanation.walkthrough: Liam Gallagher, Oasis's famously brash frontman, fits 'jumped-up', which is British for self-important; in the wordplay the phrase only turns him round.
explanation.definitionFit: Hate mail is abusive letters or messages sent to someone, spiteful material delivered by post.

clue.text: See 2
Bear on a Piano by surreal painter

indicators.note: by means next to, so the jumbled painter follows the first two pieces

parts.note: used as printed

indicators.note: surreal means bizarrely distorted, so the letters of 'painter' are rearranged

parts.note: p = piano, soft, in musical notation
anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: The title of a surrealist canvas showing a bear sitting on a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear on a Piano' reads like a Dalí-style picture title; 'bear on' is the definition, a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To appertain to something is to relate or belong to it, just as a matter can bear on a question.

clue.text: X's house arrest finally overturned

indicators.note: overturned means upside down, so the house and the letter together are read backwards

parts.note: a semi is a semi-detached house, very common in Britain

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word just before, 'arrest'

parts.note: the last letter of 'arrest'

explanation.surface: Someone called X whose house arrest was eventually quashed on appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'X's' looks like a person's name in the possessive; it is the plural of the multiplication sign. A semi is a British house sharing one wall with its neighbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The multiplication sign is read aloud as 'times', so several of those signs are called by that word.
